world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Zhao Yanzhen. 2012. Zhaozhuang Baiyu cankao yufa [Reference grammar of Zhaozhuang Bai]; Allen, Bryan. 2007. Bai Dialect Survey (SIL, access 403)

sources.citation: WALS Online, language 'Bai' (wals_code_bai, glottocode cent2004; sources Dell 1981, Wiersma 2003, Xu & Zhao 1984)
sources.note: No datapoint for 14A Fixed Stress Locations or 15A Weight-Sensitive Stress (both return 404).

sources.citation: Edmondson, Jerold A., John H. Esling & Li Shaoni. 2020. Jianchuan Bai (Illustrations of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 51(3): 491-499 (online 27 Apr 2020). doi:10.1017/S0025100319000379
sources.note: Nothing on stress (the word occurs only in a reference title). Describes 5 pitch contrasts x lax/tense register for Jianchuan (Central Bai, jian1239, not Southern); p. 498 Conventions: 'A reduced [ə] occurs morphophonemically in the second syllable of words where that syllable bears a particle relationship to the first syllable'.

sources.citation: Allen, Bryan. 2007. Bai Dialect Survey. SIL Electronic Survey Report 2007-012. Dallas: SIL International. (= Allen & Zhang Xia 2004, Yunnan Nationalities Publishing House)
sources.note: Nothing. Appendix 2 'Phonological Descriptions of Dialects Investigated' (pp. 35ff) gives syllable canon (CV), consonant/vowel charts and tones for each site incl. Zhoucheng (Dali, Southern Bai); tone section says southern varieties have 6-8 pitch-contour tones and 'tense was not a significant feature in the southern dialect variety'; the only hit for 'stress/accent' is 'they never lose their Dali accent' (regional accent).

sources.citation: Wiersma, Grace. 2003. Yunnan Bai. In Graham Thurgood & Randy J. LaPolla (eds), The Sino-Tibetan Languages, 651-673. London: Routledge.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: library print copy (Scan & Deliver or loan); the journal or volume is held, not the item itself: WID WID-LC PL3521.S56 2017
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Sec. 2.1 (p. 654): 'Syllables in the Bai language are invariably open and every syllable is considered to be tone-bearing'; sec. 2.2 Suprasegmentals covers only tones and phonation types (Jianchuan 8 tones; Dali has a reduced inventory of six tonal reflexes and a rhotic final in one syllable class).

sources.citation: Namkung, Ju (ed.). 1996. Phonological Inventories of Tibeto-Burman Languages. STEDT Monograph 3. Berkeley. Bai: Dali entries pp. 30-34 (digests of Dell 1981 [FD-Bai] pp. 21-35 and Xu & Zhao 1984 [JZ-Bai] pp. 4-12, 117-123; Sun et al. 1991 ZMYYC #35 Xizhou)
sources.note: No stress statement. Reports Dell 1981's 8 Dali tones, his pre-pausal vs non-pre-pausal syllable distinction (p. 29), tone mergers in non-pre-pausal position, and T7 'in all other contexts... realized as a short, low tone which gives the auditory impression similar to that of the Pekingese neutral tone when it follows a syllable in fourth tone' (Dell 1981: 32).

sources.citation: Edmondson, Jerold A. & Li Shaoni. 1994. Voice quality and voice quality change in the Bai language of Yunnan Province. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 17(2): 49-68.
sources.note: Nothing on word stress ('stress' only as a verb). Jianchuan Bai tones/phonation types; sec. 5 'Tone and voice quality sandhi' (pp. 65-66) describes contextual pitch and voice-quality changes (e.g. before interrogative particle mo).

sources.citation: Wikipedia (en) 'Bai language' and Wikipedia (zh) '白語'
sources.note: Nothing on stress/重音/轻声; zh article gives Jianchuan (Jinhua) and Dali (Xizhou) initials, finals and 8 tones with the Dali-only 32 tone.
